questions.title: What exactly is the definition of hyperspherical energy used in OFT, and why this particular form?
questions.question_body: In the paper, hyperspherical energy for a weight matrix is defined as HE(W) = \(\sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\), where \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i = \mathbf{w}_i / \|\mathbf{w}_i\|\). Many prior works use angular similarity (like sums over cosine similarity) or Coulomb-like potentials with different exponents. Why do the authors choose \(\|u - v\|^{-1}\) in particular instead of, say, \(1 - \cos \theta\) or \(\|u - v\|^{-2}\)? What properties of this specific potential are crucial for preserving "semantic generation ability" in diffusion models?

questions.title: Does preserving hyperspherical energy imply preserving all pairwise angles, or is the invariance only one-way?
questions.question_body: OFT argues that applying the same orthogonal transform \(\mathbf{R}\) to all neurons preserves pairwise cosine similarities and hence the hyperspherical energy. But the optimization in Eq. (1) only minimizes the difference of the scalar energy HE(W), not each pairwise angle. Is preserving the scalar HE sufficient to ensure that pairwise angles are unchanged, or could two different configurations with different pairwise angles share the same energy value? If the latter, why is energy preservation alone a reliable proxy for semantic preservation?

questions.title: Why does an orthogonal left-multiplication \(\mathbf{W} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\) change model behavior rather than just reparameterizing features?
questions.question_body: For a fully connected layer with output \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\), pre-multiplying \(\mathbf{W}^0\) by an orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\) yields \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{W}^0)^\top (\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{x})\). If the input \(\mathbf{x}\) to that layer is produced by earlier layers that are unchanged, this looks like replacing \(\mathbf{x}\) by a rotated \(\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{x}\). Shouldn't this be largely equivalent to just reparameterizing internal coordinates? In a deep U-Net with LayerNorm, residuals, and attention, how does left-multiplying individual layers by orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\) alter the function instead of canceling out across layers?

questions.title: Is there a simple proof that HE(W) is invariant under common orthogonal transforms?
questions.question_body: Given \(\mathbf{W} = [\mathbf{w}_1, \dots, \mathbf{w}_n]\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i = \mathbf{w}_i/\|\mathbf{w}_i\|\), HE is \(\sum_{i\ne j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\). If we set \(\mathbf{W}' = \mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}\) with orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\), then \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}'_i = \mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i\). Because \(\|\mathbf{R}u - \mathbf{R}v\| = \|u - v\|\), it seems HE(\(\mathbf{W}'\)) = HE(\(\mathbf{W}\)). Is this the full intended argument, or are there subtle issues with column-wise normalization when some \(\mathbf{w}_i\) are very small or nearly collinear?

questions.title: How does OFT handle biases and normalization parameters that also affect semantics?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on transforming weight matrices \(\mathbf{W}^0\) by an orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\). Many layers include biases, LayerNorm scale/shift, and attention-specific projections (Q, K, V, O) plus residual paths. Are biases and normalization parameters left untouched? If so, could this partially break the angle-preservation intuition at the feature level? Have the authors tried orthogonal finetuning for biases or normalization parameters, or is there a reason they must remain fixed?

questions.title: Cayley transform in COFT: which matrix norm does the \(\epsilon\)-constraint use and how is projection implemented?
questions.question_body: COFT imposes \(\|\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{I}\| \le \epsilon\), then approximates via Neumann series that \(\mathbf{R} \approx \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{Q}\) where \(\mathbf{Q}\) is skew-symmetric in the Cayley transform \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\). Which specific norm is used for the constraint (spectral or Frobenius)? How is the projection step implemented on \(\mathbf{Q}\) to ensure \(\|\mathbf{Q}\| \le \epsilon'\)? Is there any stability issue if \(\|\mathbf{Q}\|\) approaches 1 due to the inverse \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\)?

questions.title: Under what conditions does the Neumann series approximation for COFT hold in practice?
questions.question_body: The COFT derivation uses a Neumann series to argue \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \mathbf{Q}^k\), leading to \(\mathbf{R} \approx \mathbf{I} + 2\mathbf{Q} + \mathcal{O}(\mathbf{Q}^2)\). This requires \(\|\mathbf{Q}\| < 1\) in the operator norm. What range of \(\epsilon'\) is used so that this approximation is accurate enough during training? Does the implementation actually rely on the approximation, or is the exact inverse computed with autograd, with the Neumann series only used for intuition?

questions.title: Parameter-count comparison with LoRA: are the stated complexities apples-to-apples?
questions.question_body: The paper says LoRA has \(r'(d+n)\) trainable params for a \(d\times n\) weight and OFT has roughly \(\mathcal{O}(d^2/r)\) with \(r\) blocks, or \(\mathcal{O}(d^2/r^2)\) if blocks are shared, independent of \(n\). But LoRA often targets specific projections (e.g., Q, K, V, O) with different \(d\) and \(n\), and sometimes ties ranks across them. In practical SD v1.5 attention layers, for typical values (e.g., \(d=n=128\)), can you show a detailed per-layer and whole-model parameter breakdown for OFT vs LoRA to confirm the claimed advantages?

questions.title: How is OFT applied to convolution layers exactly, and how does block-diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\) map to spatial kernels?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that for convolution layers, using the same number of blocks as input channels makes each block transform a unique channel, akin to depth-wise convs. Convolutional kernels have shape \((C_{out}, C_{in}, k_h, k_w)\). When reshaped as a matrix, which dimension is \(d\) (the one that \(\mathbf{R}\) left-multiplies), and which dimension corresponds to the columns/neurons? Do we flatten \((C_{in} \cdot k_h \cdot k_w)\) as \(d\) and treat \(C_{out}\) as \(n\)? How is \(\mathbf{R}\) implemented efficiently in this setting without large memory overhead?

questions.title: What layers are actually finetuned with OFT in the U-Net, and why only attention weights?
questions.question_body: The paper says that for fair comparison to LoRA, OFT is applied to the same attention weights. Which projections specifically are transformed (Q, K, V, O, and/or linear layers in cross-attention blocks)? Is there any ablation showing results when applying OFT to MLP or convolution blocks in SD v1.5? If OFT is architecture-agnostic, why not show the benefit on non-attention components where a large fraction of parameters reside?

questions.title: How can OFT enable controllable generation without adding inference-time modules like ControlNet?
questions.question_body: ControlNet introduces an auxiliary branch conditioned on control signals (e.g., edges or segmentation maps). The paper claims OFT introduces no inference overhead and still enables controllability. How is the control signal injected into the base SD v1.5 model if no extra branch or adapter is added? Are you finetuning cross-attention conditioning to also attend to the control map embeddings? If so, what is the encoder for control signals at training and inference time, and is it part of the base model or an external frozen feature extractor?

questions.title: Could preserving hyperspherical energy fail when neurons are duplicated, since the energy has singularities?
questions.question_body: HE is \(\sum_{i\ne j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\). If some normalized neurons are nearly identical, \(\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i - \hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|\) is near zero and HE can blow up. Do pretrained diffusion models have such near-duplicate neurons? If so, how is HE computed stably? Is there any regularization like adding a small \(\delta\) to denominators, and if so, does that preserve the orthogonal invariance property used by OFT?

questions.title: Is there empirical evidence that angle (direction) dominates magnitude for diffusion U-Net weights, beyond the autoencoder toy example?
questions.question_body: The paper shows a toy autoencoder where using only angular information at test time reconstructs semantics, while magnitudes alone do not. But SD v1.5 is a diffusion U-Net with attention and normalization. Is there a layer-wise ablation showing that rotating neuron directions (keeping magnitudes) accounts for most of the semantic change in text-to-image tasks? For example, can you quantify performance when only angles change vs when only magnitudes change for attention and conv layers?

questions.title: COFT’s "radius constraint to the hypersphere": what hypersphere is this exactly?
questions.question_body: The abstract mentions that COFT imposes "an additional radius constraint to the hypersphere." In the method, COFT constrains \(\|\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{I}\| \le \epsilon\), which is a ball on the manifold of orthogonal matrices around \(\mathbf{I}\), not a sphere of neuron vectors. Could the authors clarify the terminology: is the "hypersphere" here the unit sphere in parameter space of \(\mathbf{R}\), or the sphere for normalized neurons? How should we interpret \(\epsilon\) geometrically?

questions.title: Re-scaled OFT: why constrain the diagonal scales to be positive, and does scaling preserve HE?
questions.question_body: The re-scaled variant learns a diagonal \(\mathbf{D}=\mathrm{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n)\) with \(s_i>0\), applying \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\mathbf{D})^\top \mathbf{x}\). Since HE uses normalized columns \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i\), scaling any column leaves HE unchanged. But are there any subtle issues if we allow negative scaling (sign flips), which can be absorbed by an orthogonal reflection? Also, if we scale columns that later feed into LayerNorm, could this interact with normalization statistics in ways that alter training stability?

questions.title: LoRA vs OFT: when is \((\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0\) effectively low-rank?
questions.question_body: The paper notes OFT’s forward pass can be written as \((\mathbf{W}^0 + (\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\) and that if \(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\) is low-rank then the update resembles LoRA. For a block-diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\) with \(r\) blocks, what is the rank of \(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\) in general? Under what settings (e.g., shared blocks) does OFT tend to produce updates with low effective rank, and can we quantify this vs LoRA’s explicit rank \(r'\)?

questions.title: How sensitive is OFT to the block count \(r\) and to sharing blocks across dimensions?
questions.question_body: The method reduces parameters by using an \(r\)-block diagonal \(\mathbf{R}\), optionally sharing blocks to reach \(\mathcal{O}(d^2/r^2)\) parameters. How do different \(r\) values affect controllability, subject fidelity, and convergence stability? Is there a rule-of-thumb to choose \(r\) per layer size \(d\)? Are there failure cases where too aggressive block sharing produces artifacts or collapses?

questions.title: What norm preservation properties of orthogonal transforms matter most for diffusion training?
questions.question_body: Orthogonal matrices preserve vector norms and pairwise angles. In diffusion U-Nets, stability and Lipschitz properties are important for training. Is there any evidence that OFT’s norm-preserving updates (as opposed to general small Euclidean updates) reduce gradient explosion/vanishing or improve conditioning of attention layers? Any comparisons with spectral normalization or orthogonal weight regularization baselines?

questions.title: Details of the control consistency metrics: how do you prevent reward hacking?
questions.question_body: For Canny-to-image (C2I) and Seg-to-image (S2I), the paper measures alignment by extracting edges or segmentations from the generated image and comparing to the input control via IoU/F1. Models could learn to produce images that specifically fool the edge/segmentation extractor. Do you observe such reward hacking? What extractor models are used (frozen off-the-shelf?), and are there ablations showing that better control consistency correlates with human-judged controllability and not gaming the metric?

questions.title: What is the training loss used under OFT/COFT for subject-driven generation and control tasks?
questions.question_body: The paper says OFT follows DreamBooth for subject-driven generation and ControlNet/T2I-Adapter settings for controllable generation, but it is unclear what exact training loss is used. For DreamBooth, is it the reconstruction loss plus class-specific prior preservation (as in the original paper), unchanged? For control tasks, are you simply conditioning the diffusion U-Net on control inputs (how?) and using the standard diffusion denoising objective? Any additional regularizers to encourage controllability under OFT?

questions.title: Do the claimed data-efficiency gains hold at matched compute and augmentation settings?
questions.question_body: The paper shows OFT reaches good performance with fewer images or epochs compared to ControlNet and LoRA. Are these comparisons run with identical batch sizes, augmentation policies, text prompts, and optimizer schedules? For example, in the ADE20K S2I task, could ControlNet benefit from stronger data augmentation or longer warm-up to close the gap, or is OFT consistently superior even when compute budgets are matched?

questions.title: How is numerical stability of the Cayley inverse handled for large \(d\) and during backprop?
questions.question_body: OFT uses \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with skew-symmetric \(\mathbf{Q}\). In practice, when \(d\) is large (e.g., 512 or 1024), inverting \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\) repeatedly in training could introduce numerical instability. Are there specific linear algebra tricks (e.g., LU with pivoting, solving linear systems instead of explicit inverse) and gradient clipping or conditioning techniques used to keep training stable?

questions.title: What happens if the pretrained weight \(\mathbf{W}^0\) is not full-rank?
questions.question_body: Some arguments comparing OFT to LoRA assume \(\mathbf{W}^0\) is full-rank. However, due to architectural redundancies or training quirks, certain layers may be rank-deficient. In that case, how does OFT’s update \((\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I})\mathbf{W}^0\) behave, and does it limit the expressive power compared to LoRA’s explicit low-rank additive updates?

questions.title: Compositionality of multiple OFT transforms: since orthogonal matrices don't commute, how is order handled?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions a compositionality potential: multiply orthogonal matrices from multiple finetuning tasks to combine skills. But in general, \(\mathbf{R}_1\mathbf{R}_2 \neq \mathbf{R}_2\mathbf{R}_1\). If we learn OFT matrices for two tasks A and B, does the composed model depend on whether we apply \(\mathbf{R}_A\) then \(\mathbf{R}_B\) or vice versa? Is there a canonical order, or could we constrain the parameterization (e.g., block structure) so they commute and avoid order dependence?

questions.title: How do OFT and COFT behave across different diffusion timesteps and noise levels?
questions.question_body: Diffusion model behavior varies by timestep. Are the learned \(\mathbf{R}\) matrices implicitly adapting the model more at certain timesteps? Have you inspected per-timestep losses or guidance strength to see if OFT changes early-noise denoising vs late denoising differently? Could one consider timestep-dependent orthogonal finetuning for finer control?

questions.title: Does preserving HE per layer guarantee preservation of global inter-layer structure?
questions.question_body: OFT preserves HE of each transformed layer individually. But semantic information may rely on cross-layer alignments (e.g., how certain directions in one layer align with directions in the next). Is there any measurement of inter-layer angular consistency before and after OFT? Could preserving per-layer HE still disrupt global geometry, and if so, would adding constraints on cross-layer relationships help or overconstrain the system?

questions.title: In the toy autoencoder experiment, what exact "angular activation" was applied at test time?
questions.question_body: The figure description mentions replacing inner product with angular or magnitude-only computations at test time, without training with cosine activation. What precisely was computed for the angular-only case? Was it \(z = \cos(\angle(\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x}))\), i.e., normalized dot product? Or some monotonic function of the angle? Could you provide the exact formulas used for the three test-time variants?

questions.title: How is subject preservation quantified, and how sensitive are DINO/CLIP-I to pose and background changes?
questions.question_body: Subject fidelity is measured with DINO and CLIP-I similarities between generated and real images. For DreamBooth-style personalization, changes in pose or background can affect these metrics. Are these metrics normalized for pose/lighting? Have you performed ablations to ensure OFT’s higher scores are not due to producing images closer in low-level features (e.g., background) rather than genuinely preserving subject identity?

questions.title: Why not minimize hyperspherical energy during finetuning if uniformity is good for generalization?
questions.question_body: The paper argues minimizing HE (which favors uniform neuron directions) can destroy pretrained semantics in diffusion models, unlike the classification setting in prior work. Could you provide empirical or theoretical evidence showing that directly minimizing HE during finetuning degrades text-to-image performance (e.g., shows identity drift or loss of controllability)? Are there cases where a very mild HE reduction helps regularize overfitting without damaging semantics?

questions.title: How are hyperparameters \(\epsilon\) (COFT) and block count \(r\) selected in practice?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests COFT is less sensitive to learning rate and iteration count with a proper \(\epsilon\). In practical workflows, how do you set \(\epsilon\) and \(r\) per layer? Is there an automated schedule for \(\epsilon\) (e.g., annealing) that improves stability? Any guidance on per-layer \(\epsilon\) based on layer depth, width \(d\), or role (self vs cross attention)?

questions.title: Is there truly zero inference overhead when control signals must be ingested?
questions.question_body: The paper claims no additional inference overhead. But for controllable generation (e.g., edges or segmentation maps), the model must process the control signal somehow. Does that require an extra encoder, or is the control preprocessed into the text prompt or into fixed positional embeddings? If an encoder is used, is it reused from existing model components (thus not adding parameters), or is it external and frozen so the U-Net’s forward pass remains unchanged?

questions.title: How does OFT interact with EMA weights and classifier-free guidance at inference?
questions.question_body: Stable Diffusion often uses EMA (exponential moving average) weights for better sampling, and classifier-free guidance at inference. When finetuning via OFT, do you apply the orthogonal transform to the EMA weights, or re-derive EMA after finetuning? Does OFT change the effective guidance scale sensitivity, and did you need to retune guidance scale for best results?
